summary.core_quantum_assessment: No mathematical error was demonstrated in the reviewed core quantum argument. Three local exposition wording/exercise errors are separated from clarification, pedagogy and evidence-interface concerns.

locator.quote: We give the complete argument with explicit constants

feedback.feedback: The opening promises a complete argument, but §1.3 later exempts the Forrelation supplier, parts of the construction, standard amplification, and several refinements proved only in the record. A specialist cannot tell from the abstract which result is actually proved in this document and which is supplied as a lemma.
feedback.why_it_matters: The reader starts auditing a self-contained paper and only later learns its intended dependency boundary.
feedback.advice: Describe the companion as proving the separation from stated ingredients, and distinguish the detailed reconstruction in the record. Keep the exceptions in one short, clearly labelled dependency paragraph; do not add review-status disclaimers.

locator.quote: comparisons need to be reliable only for the winner

feedback.feedback: This is the most useful sentence in the abstract. It singles out the precise obstacle that prevents a routine reduction to an ordinary comparison problem.
feedback.why_it_matters: A quantum-algorithms reader can immediately identify the hypothesis that makes the new tournament worth inspecting.
feedback.advice: Protect this sentence through cuts, and make it the organising claim of the quantum overview.

locator.quote: in each of a constant fraction of the columns

feedback.feedback: The phrasing can sound like a deterministic per-column necessity. The proof actually bounds a low-budget algorithm under a hard distribution by dividing columns into heavy ones and light ones whose correct address is unlikely to be guessed.
feedback.why_it_matters: The informal statement is stronger than the event-based claim the lower-bound argument needs, and obscures why the direct product and the random planted column both matter.
feedback.advice: Give this as a hard-distribution intuition, or say that a small total budget leaves most possible planted columns with too little address information. Avoid suggesting that every successful execution literally solves that many addresses.

locator.quote: reads its input one bit at a time

feedback.feedback: The first sentence uses familiar classical reading language before giving the correct quantum oracle. A quantum query can have its index register in superposition; it does not reveal one classical bit to the algorithm at each step. This is conventional shorthand, but a more literal opening would remove the need to reinterpret it.
feedback.why_it_matters: The paper immediately supplies the correct oracle, but the opening sentence makes the reader mentally undo a familiar misleading picture.
feedback.advice: Introduce access through a bit oracle and the charge per oracle call. Reserve the language of reading a particular position for classical trees.

locator.section: §1 Introduction, Theorem 1 and the next paragraph
locator.quote: Taking $k=3$ in (2) gives exponent $10/3>3$

feedback.feedback: The concrete k=3 consequence gives a quick reason this is a strict advance beyond the cubic relation, before the limiting quantifier argument.
feedback.why_it_matters: It distinguishes refuting the cubic conjecture from the separate task of identifying the infimum of all universal exponents.
feedback.advice: Keep the numerical witness here and the full fixed-k quantifier argument in §6.

locator.quote: This paper adds the following to the preprint.

feedback.feedback: The four-part contribution paragraph mixes huge explicit constants, a common-circuit issue, counterexamples, two observations, the record, a uniform Forrelation bound and Lean. In the PDF it continues onto page 2 before the reader has seen the construction. These are not equally important reasons for a quantum specialist to read on.
feedback.why_it_matters: The central algorithmic idea competes with a catalogue of supporting deliverables and refinements.
feedback.advice: Lead with what the companion explains better: arbitrary-probability comparisons and the assembly of the two bounds. Move the numerical threshold and constant list next to the bounds they quantify; mention the other additions in a shorter contribution paragraph.

locator.quote: including a Forrelation lower bound uniform in $k$

feedback.feedback: The uniform estimate is buried in the description of the record, although §5 later says it has a different proof route and a better k-dependence than the cited Bansal–Sinha estimate. That is a substantive quantitative refinement and should not first appear as a supporting-document feature.
feedback.why_it_matters: A reader cannot separate the original separation theorem, the companion’s exposition, and the record’s additional quantitative work.
feedback.advice: Name the uniform estimate as an additional result of the record, with its exact role in the growing-k remark. Preserve OpenAI’s credit for the original function and separation analysis; do not market the refinement as a new separation theorem.

locator.quote: Q=\widetilde O\bigl(m'+\sqrt{nm'}\bigr)

feedback.feedback: The displayed cost suppresses Q(g) before the following sentence assumes it is polylogarithmic. With a general partial g, the evaluation contribution in the cited construction is m′Q(g), up to the stated logarithmic overhead.
feedback.why_it_matters: A specialist checking the conversion has to supply a hypothesis retroactively; the display is otherwise not the count just described.
feedback.advice: Move the polylogarithmic-Q(g) assumption before this display, or include Q(g) in the display and simplify afterwards. This is a local scope repair, not a challenge to the historical exponents.

locator.quote: Exponent $a$ with $R=Q^{a}$ (total $f$)

feedback.feedback: The table heading uses equality for separation lower bounds, while its last row is an upper bound holding for every total function.
feedback.why_it_matters: Two different logical directions are compressed into one heading, precisely where the reader is comparing the historical endpoints.
feedback.advice: Label the separation rows by their achieved lower-bound exponent and put the universal upper bound in a visibly separate final row or sentence.

locator.quote: Tal's bound for $k$-fold Rorrelation

feedback.feedback: Rorrelation appears before the text explains that it uses an orthogonal matrix rather than the explicit Walsh matrix. At this point it can look like a typographical variant of Forrelation.
feedback.why_it_matters: A reader who knows Forrelation but has not followed the partial-separation literature may miss the distinction that later justifies the exact circuit.
feedback.advice: Add a short parenthetical description on first use and let §1.3 carry the precise contrast.

locator.quote: the AND–OR recipe stops at the cube

feedback.feedback: The current formulation correctly limits the barrier to the displayed construction and explains 5/2, 8/3 and 3 with one parameter c. This is a successful repair of the earlier historical discussion.
feedback.why_it_matters: It explains what the new construction must change without asserting an impossibility theorem for all cheat-sheet ideas.
feedback.advice: Keep the qualified scope and the common conversion calculation; do not replace it with an unsupported claim that all previous methods were incapable of going beyond three.

locator.quote: The answers $s_i=(P(A_{i,1}),\dots,P(A_{i,r}))$ select one cell

feedback.feedback: The overview assigns an address to every column before mentioning that P is partial. On a total input some of these vectors do not exist.
feedback.why_it_matters: This temporarily erases the off-promise case that is the source of the quantum algorithm’s difficulty.
feedback.advice: Say at this first use that the true address exists when the column’s instances are promised. Later distinguish it from the decoder’s always-defined output label.

locator.quote: Column $i^\star$ is the winner:

feedback.feedback: Figure 1 is an effective layout, but its internal label calls the r address blocks independent instances. The total function imposes no distribution or independence; only the hard distribution in §4 does. The word is not needed to explain disjoint coordinates.
feedback.why_it_matters: The drawing can silently transfer a probabilistic assumption into the deterministic definition.
feedback.advice: Use disjoint address blocks in the diagram and reserve independent for the sampled blocks of the lower-bound distribution. Keep the outward arrows and selected-cell emphasis.

locator.quote: which takes about $m^2$ queries.

feedback.feedback: The heuristic makes the erased-zero obstacle resemble ordinary search over m² unrelated bits. Here there is one zero per dummy column and the planted index is independent; the key identity is E[Z]/m, not simply a generic OR lower bound.
feedback.why_it_matters: The reader may misunderstand where the extra factor m comes from and why independence of the planted index is indispensable.
feedback.advice: Give one clause connecting the heuristic to the number of columns whose zero has actually been discovered, with a forward reference to (11). Keep the detailed proof in §4.3.

locator.section: §1.2 Overview, order of the two mechanisms
locator.quote: For the classical lower bound we compare a zero-input

feedback.feedback: The overview spends two dense paragraphs on the lower bound before explaining the nonstandard quantum search, even though the abstract and §3 identify that search as the point a quantum reader should inspect.
feedback.why_it_matters: The motivating question—why cheap address decoding does not immediately make Grover search cheap—is answered late.
feedback.advice: Consider introducing the nested-search cost and the comparison remedy immediately after Figure 1, then give the planted-distribution intuition. This is an ordering suggestion for this audience, not a demand that every version use the same order.

locator.quote: a total cost of about $\sqrt m\cdot\sqrt K\approx m$

feedback.feedback: The failed nested-search count explains why the tournament is necessary. It turns a list of ingredients into an algorithmic design problem.
feedback.why_it_matters: Without this bottleneck the reader might think the theorem follows by applying Grover search to the winner predicate.
feedback.advice: Keep the cost comparison close to the first account of the algorithm and refer back to it when verification is deferred.

locator.section: §1.3 Relation to earlier constructions, comparison paragraph
locator.quote: king finding [@MPS2023] searches a fixed tournament

feedback.feedback: The paragraph names king finding without specifying the output property. A king need only reach every vertex within two directed edges; a dominant candidate here must beat every opponent with high probability, and a listed candidate still needs verification.
feedback.why_it_matters: The three tasks can look interchangeable simply because all use pairwise comparisons.
feedback.advice: Give the output contract of king finding in a short clause, and compare contracts rather than only naming the graph models.

locator.section: §1.3 Relation to earlier constructions, comparison paragraph
locator.quote: Quantum search with bounded-error inputs [@HMW2003] likewise needs every comparison

feedback.feedback: Høyer–Mosca–de Wolf formulate search over fixed target bits with bounded-error algorithms for those bits; their theorem is not specifically a comparison theorem. Here it can be used after a candidate is converted into a genuine verification predicate, but cannot simply interpret arbitrary loser-pair probabilities as noisy orientations.
feedback.why_it_matters: The current shorthand risks making a precise hypothesis distinction sound like a blanket dismissal of bounded-error search.
feedback.advice: Name the fixed target predicate and the cost of evaluating it. Explain that the obstacle is applying that primitive directly to the cheap pairwise comparison, rather than the impossibility of using bounded-error search anywhere.

locator.section: §1.3 Relation to earlier constructions, comparison paragraph
locator.quote: in each a comparison has a fixed intended outcome.

feedback.feedback: This is the right contrast, but the paper leaves the relation among total orders, fixed tournaments, approximate fixed-edge evaluation and arbitrary pair probabilities entirely in a dense paragraph.
feedback.why_it_matters: A reader must reconstruct which assumptions each cited algorithm shares with Proposition 3.
feedback.advice: Use a small comparison of input contract, output contract and relevant invariant, or a short progression through those four cases. Keep it limited to the cited algorithms actually inspected.

locator.section: §1.3 Relation to earlier constructions, final paragraph
locator.quote: Every other link to the record points to a longer version

feedback.feedback: The paragraph combining the roadmap, external inputs, record-only refinements, scope of every remaining link and the exposition reads like a navigation contract rather than the end of an introduction.
feedback.why_it_matters: It delays §2 and asks the reader to retain a classification of links before encountering the corresponding mathematics.
feedback.advice: Separate a short mathematical dependency statement from a one-sentence roadmap. Put detailed link classification in the record or repository navigation; keep no bureaucratic disclaimers in the paper.

locator.quote: It prepares $u$, applies the product in (3)

feedback.feedback: The cost statement does not locally explain that each diagonal sign matrix uses one phase query to the standard bit oracle, while H, the uniform state and the projection are input-independent operations. That is the short bridge from the displayed linear algebra to O_k queries.
feedback.why_it_matters: A specialist can supply the bridge, but a companion claiming to expose the argument should make the oracle accounting visible at its first essential use.
feedback.advice: Add the one-query-per-sign-layer explanation and specify right-to-left application order. The original preprint supplies exactly these details in Lemma 2.1; no circuit diagram or gate count is needed.

locator.quote: The interference test of Aaronson and Ambainis

feedback.feedback: The text explicitly says that the sign-sensitive interference test would also work and explains why promise membership is certified elsewhere. This prevents the projection experiment from being mistaken for a uniquely necessary decoder.
feedback.why_it_matters: It connects the presentation to the form of Forrelation familiar to specialists and identifies which decoder property the construction consumes.
feedback.advice: Keep this comparison and the on-promise/off-promise distinction, while avoiding an expanded survey of all equivalent tests.

locator.quote: An exact fan-in-two Boolean circuit $\mathcal C$

feedback.feedback: The definition of S does not explicitly say whether it counts input nodes or only non-input gates, including the output gates. The cell size rS and K=r(S+2)+2m−1 later use the latter convention.
feedback.why_it_matters: A reader checking the transcript length has to infer a counting convention that the original preprint states explicitly.
feedback.advice: Define S as the number of non-input gates, including the output gates, once. This also explains why gate checks and the two output-value checks are distinct.

locator.quote: All of these are independent input bits.

feedback.feedback: Independence is a property of a probability law, whereas this paragraph is defining the coordinates of a total Boolean function. The intended point is that cells contain separately supplied bits, rather than transcripts generated automatically from the A-blocks.
feedback.why_it_matters: The phrasing is especially risky because independence later becomes a real hypothesis of the direct-product argument.
feedback.advice: Say that these are separate, unconstrained input coordinates and that alleged transcripts may be wrong. Reserve probabilistic independence for §4.

locator.quote: both bounds in (2) are proved for the function built from it.

feedback.feedback: Fixing the circuit before both analyses is a valuable precision point: changing the transcript circuit changes the total function’s coordinates.
feedback.why_it_matters: It prevents a seemingly innocent combination of an upper bound for one construction with a lower bound for another.
feedback.advice: Keep the mathematical point in §2. Later formal quantifiers can link back to it instead of restating the same reassurance several times.

locator.quote: so in terms of its input length

feedback.feedback: The n-exponent is a useful secondary fact but is not used in either analysis or the optimal-power deduction. It appears between the function definition and the local-test mechanism, where the reader is trying to understand how a certificate can be checked cheaply.
feedback.why_it_matters: It interrupts the construction-to-algorithm dependency with an asymptotic change of variable.
feedback.advice: Move the input-length observation into a remark after the two complexity bounds or a short note at the end of §2. State explicitly that k is fixed in this conversion.

locator.quote: The circuit size enters the quantum bound only through the cost $\sqrt K$

feedback.feedback: This sentence is an excellent explanation of why the circuit must be small even though the quantum algorithm does not evaluate all its gates directly.
feedback.why_it_matters: It separates the cost of generating a certificate from the cost of checking a supplied transcript.
feedback.advice: Keep this sentence at the end of the local-test paragraph; it is more useful than additional exact gate-count arithmetic.

locator.quote: Each trial chooses, with probability $1/2$ each

feedback.feedback: Round six planned a two-sentence amplification sketch. The current proof still walks through M, a two-case success estimate, 9/20, 9/40 and repeated trials before the new comparison mechanism appears. Those constants are standard supporting machinery, while the exact successful-label law is the property later used.
feedback.why_it_matters: A quantum specialist spends attention on a familiar implementation before reaching the novel invariant; the priority of the previous revision has not fully survived.
feedback.advice: Retain the fixed-cap contract, state preservation and a concise explanation of randomized Grover counts plus fresh retries. Leave the numerical trial calculation in record §5.1 and cite BHMT/BBHT locally.

locator.quote: Search with an unknown success probability bounds its cost only in expectation

feedback.feedback: The sentence is broader than its cited result. BHMT Theorem 3 is an expected-cost QSearch algorithm; fixed timeouts and bounded-error worst-case search are already standard in BBHT and Dürr–Høyer. A known lower threshold on p allows the capped form used here.
feedback.why_it_matters: The wording can make a routine truncation device sound like a previously unavailable feature of quantum search.
feedback.advice: Refer specifically to the untruncated QSearch theorem being contrasted, and say what the threshold γ and fixed retry budget add for this application. Do not claim that unknown-p search in general only has expected bounds.

locator.quote: Below we use only the distribution of the label measured after a success

feedback.feedback: This sentence makes the operational need clear without denying the stronger state-preserving mathematical lemma. It is a successful correction of the earlier conflation.
feedback.why_it_matters: The reader can follow the sampler using ordinary conditional probabilities once the coherent trial is finished.
feedback.advice: Keep it adjacent to the lemma, and make the record’s corresponding finite-label discussion agree with the separate measured/reset implementation described in §7.

locator.quote: For an unordered pair $\{i,j\}$, we sort the indices

feedback.feedback: Sorting the pair before running one circuit is the right concrete reason for a_ij+a_ji=1. Complementarity is a semantic property of the same experiment, not an assumption about two independently designed decoders.
feedback.why_it_matters: The drift identity depends exactly on this symmetry, even for off-promise rivals.
feedback.advice: Preserve the construction and the explicit self-loss convention through compression.

locator.quote: If exactly one column disqualifies the other, it is the victor;

feedback.feedback: This rule has two binary observations and two tie cases, but it is encoded in a long procedural sentence. A reader checking the tie-break counterexample must reconstruct the four possible outputs.
feedback.why_it_matters: It is easy to reverse which pointer bit disqualifies which column.
feedback.advice: Give a compact four-case description, or state the two pointer bits first and then the winning condition. Link the smallest-index tie to the false-dominant example in Appendix A.

locator.quote: The decoded labels stay in orthogonal registers

feedback.feedback: This explicitly justifies transferring the measured decoder probabilities into the coherent comparison circuit. It is mathematical content, not formalisation bookkeeping.
feedback.why_it_matters: Without retained labels, erasing or merging branches could alter the comparison amplitudes and invalidate the later product law.
feedback.advice: Keep the sentence and the retained-workspace requirement in Proposition 3.

locator.quote: One comparison costs $c=O_k(\ell\log\ell)$ queries.

feedback.feedback: The cost is correct from the displayed r and ε, but the paper never explicitly connects the relatively weak ε=Θ(1/log m) guarantee to the fact that comparisons are sampled as their actual probability laws. Readers accustomed to approximate-oracle composition may expect error reduction proportional to the total number of coherent calls.
feedback.why_it_matters: This is one of the most instructive differences from treating the circuit as an approximate fixed predicate.
feedback.advice: Explain that no claim is made that every comparison call is correct: a_ij are exact circuit probabilities, and only the winner’s product weight needs the 1−ε bound over T pivots. This resolves a likely error-budget question without adding another union bound.

locator.quote: A quantum algorithm with $O(c\sqrt m\,T^2\log T)$ queries

feedback.feedback: The proposition gives the crucial contract but the actual algorithm is dispersed among the ideal-process, exact-sampling and coupling paragraphs. A reader has to reconstruct when the pivot list is updated, when measurement occurs and what is returned on failure.
feedback.why_it_matters: This adds avoidable reconstruction work to the one algorithm the specialist came to understand.
feedback.advice: Put a brief numbered description beside the proposition: initial empty list; construct the trial from the measured history; amplify and measure; append or stop; return the list after at most T stages. Keep the proofs in the existing paragraphs.

locator.quote: We replace membership in that set by the weight

feedback.feedback: The set-to-weight relationship is now stated explicitly and is the best connection to the 2026 candidate-comparison literature.
feedback.why_it_matters: It shows how the familiar surviving-set invariant changes when loser comparisons do not encode fixed edges.
feedback.advice: Preserve this explanation and add a genuinely fractional example if space permits; do not re-raise the already fixed complaint that the relationship is absent.

locator.quote: the probability that $i$ beats every pivot

feedback.feedback: This phrase should be read as the probability for fresh comparison trials conditional on a fixed input and already measured pivot history. It is not a statement that the events in the adaptive ideal process are unconditionally independent.
feedback.why_it_matters: The product notation invites precisely the independence confusion that the fresh-workspace construction later resolves.
feedback.advice: Add the conditional/fresh-trial qualification here, then let the tensor-product calculation establish it. No independence assumption on the input is involved.

locator.quote: After $T$ steps $\mathbb EW\le m2^{-T}$.

feedback.feedback: The process is defined to stop when W=0, but this sentence refers to a value after T steps. The intended convention is that zero weight remains zero after stopping.
feedback.why_it_matters: The probabilistic argument is sound, but a proof-oriented reader momentarily has to complete the stopped process.
feedback.advice: Declare the stopped state absorbing, or write the bound for W after padding stopped runs by zeros. A short clause is enough.

locator.quote: No order or transitivity enters, so cycles among losers do no harm.

feedback.feedback: The statement comes immediately after the pairing identity that proves it. This is persuasive mathematical exposition: the allowed pathology is explained by the proof, not merely asserted.
feedback.why_it_matters: It identifies the invariant responsible for generality and helps a reader see why a three-cycle is harmless.
feedback.advice: Keep the identity and this consequence next to one another.

locator.quote: The algorithm never computes the weights.

feedback.feedback: This crucial statement is easy to skim past. A reader may otherwise imagine amplitude estimation of every a_ij followed by a classical weighted sample, which would destroy the query bound.
feedback.why_it_matters: It is the implementation insight that converts the classical ideal process into a cheap quantum routine.
feedback.advice: Give the sentence more prominence and tie it directly to the success-and-label mass w_i/m. A small state/flag schematic would help more than a second static picture of the input.

locator.quote: \frac1{\sqrt m}\sum_{i=1}^m|i\rangle\bigotimes_{b=1}^{n}|\phi(i,\rho_b)\rangle

feedback.feedback: The expert paper gives the exact state and mass computation but no finite example with fractional a_ij. The exposition’s new sampled stage uses only deterministic comparisons, so following the cross-document route still does not exhibit the feature that distinguishes the theorem from fixed-tournament search.
feedback.why_it_matters: The algebra is correct, but the reader never sees the weighted generalisation do something a surviving set cannot.
feedback.advice: Add or point to a tiny admissible comparison-probability matrix with a dominant candidate and a fractional loser pair, and trace one measured pivot, the resulting nonbinary weights, the total success probability and the conditional label law. Label it as an example of Proposition 3 unless a board realisation is actually supplied. One concrete abstract instance has dominant vertex 1, a_1j=1 for j≠1, a_23=1/3, a_24=3/4, a_34=2/5, reverse probabilities complementary, and diagonal zero. After pivot 2, weights are (1,0,2/3,1/4), success probability is 23/48, and the conditional label law is (12/23,0,8/23,3/23). These numbers illustrate the existing abstract proposition; they are not asserted to be realised by the supplied four-column board.

locator.quote: on reported failure we stop and return the list.

feedback.feedback: Stopping with the current list is essential for zero inputs and for histories after a dominant candidate has already been selected.
feedback.why_it_matters: It avoids silently assuming a solution exists for every amplification call or letting an unknown-probability search run indefinitely.
feedback.advice: Keep the stopped-list behaviour visible in any algorithm summary.

locator.quote: The failure probabilities may depend on the history

feedback.feedback: This is the right reason to couple conditional on the full past rather than condition globally on all stages succeeding. Exact labels at each successful stage do not make an all-success conditioned history unbiased.
feedback.why_it_matters: It protects the most delicate probabilistic transfer in the upper bound.
feedback.advice: Preserve the stagewise coupling and the fact that a failure after inclusion cannot remove the winner; avoid compressing it to a bare union-bound slogan.

locator.quote: Stage $n$ costs $O(c(n+1)\sqrt m\log(1/\varepsilon))$

feedback.feedback: The current indexing uses n for the number of previous pivots, while earlier n denoted total input length. The +1 is also padding relative to n comparison workspaces and is not explained.
feedback.why_it_matters: Neither issue changes the bound, but the reader must resolve a needless symbol collision while checking the only nontrivial query sum.
feedback.advice: Use a stage/history index such as s consistently in this subsection and say the +1 is harmless padding, including the empty history. Preparing the uniform initial state is input-independent and costs no input queries.

locator.quote: A column that beats every rival with probability at least $1-\varepsilon$ need not win

feedback.feedback: The warning is correct, but its justification is relegated to row 3 of a table after the references. This is the precise reason the algorithm returns a list for verification rather than deciding acceptance from its tournament.
feedback.why_it_matters: A quantum reader may see verification as routine overhead rather than the operation that makes the algorithm valid on every input.
feedback.advice: Give the one-sentence all-one, smallest-index false-certificate example here, with the detailed counterexample retained in Appendix A. Link it to the different meanings of comparison dominance and satisfying the total function.

locator.quote: We reject the candidate if a failing test is found and accept it otherwise

feedback.feedback: The verifier treats reported failure of the search as acceptance of the candidate. That is correct, but the words failure and success now reverse their meaning relative to candidate validity.
feedback.why_it_matters: A reader can momentarily confuse the search’s failure flag with an unreliable candidate or with a failure to run the algorithm.
feedback.advice: Name the search output as a detected violation versus no violation detected, and immediately attach the two guarantees: a true certificate has no violation; a false certificate escapes detection with probability at most ε.

locator.quote: the winner is accepted whenever its address is decoded correctly.

feedback.feedback: The ensuing one-input bound uses only one fresh decoding error, not T verification errors. This is a useful asymmetry, but the explanation is implicit.
feedback.why_it_matters: A reader may think the union bound is missing a term or try to add errors for accepting nonwinners on an input whose correct answer is already one.
feedback.advice: Say that false positives on a one-input cannot hurt the decision and that, conditional on reaching the listed winner, its fresh decoder has failure probability at most ε for every prior history.

locator.quote: The exponent six in (2) comes from a deliberately loose count

feedback.feedback: The paragraph derives the loose exponent through inflated log bounds after giving the sharper comparison cost and the tournament proposition. It forces the reader to switch accounting conventions solely to match a stated constant package.
feedback.why_it_matters: The main algorithmic cost is harder to remember than it needs to be, and routine padding receives more space than the operational sampler.
feedback.advice: Keep a small ledger of comparison, tournament and verification costs, then state that the explicit bound is padded to log^6 for the record’s constants. Move the trial-by-trial padding calculation to record §5.4 as intended in round six.

locator.quote: by compactness the best worst-case success is attained

feedback.feedback: The compactness and minimax justification is inserted into an otherwise algorithmic transition as a long final sentence. It is mathematically legitimate, but its placement makes the reader work through the existence of μ before seeing what μ will be used to hide.
feedback.why_it_matters: This slows a quantum specialist entering the classical half without helping them retain the construction.
feedback.advice: Introduce μ and its depth-L hardness property first, then give the finite minimax justification in a short parenthesis or immediately following sentence. Keep the strict L<R(P) hypothesis.

locator.quote: We work with unnormalised measures, so that branches of probability zero need no conditioning.

feedback.feedback: This is an economical explanation of the proof’s choice of formalism. The leaf factorisation and one-factor update are then enough to see why adaptive interleaving does not break the product.
feedback.why_it_matters: A quantum reader gets a complete lower-bound ingredient without a detour into a general direct-product theorem.
feedback.advice: Keep this proof and the joint-independence hypothesis; its compactness is a good model for trimming the standard amplification calculation.

locator.quote: Drucker's Theorem 1.1

feedback.feedback: The nearby discussion of exact β^r versus 2β^r is a useful historical clarification, but the full parameter substitution competes with the conclusion of the lemma.
feedback.why_it_matters: The specialist needs to know that the general theorem would suffice; they do not need to stop the proof to audit a second proof route.
feedback.advice: Keep the one-sentence sufficiency observation and send the explicit substitution to the record. Do not revive the previous incorrect suggestion that a global-budget theorem cannot apply.

locator.quote: leaves every cell blank, with all its bits zero.

feedback.feedback: Blank is helpfully defined as a fixed bit string, but a later query to the selected cell is treated as a possible discrepancy even when that particular bit agrees with zero in the planted input.
feedback.why_it_matters: A careful reader may try to interpret cell access as an exact detection event and wonder where an occupancy flag is stored.
feedback.advice: Say once that touching the cell is a sufficient event to cover all possible discrepancies, not that every such query detects the plant. No extra marker bit is present or needed.

locator.quote: They differ only at the erased zero

feedback.feedback: Figure 2 and its caption identify the two places in which the coupled inputs can differ and state that the address blocks are shared. This gives the lower-bound proof a concrete causal structure.
feedback.why_it_matters: It makes the two subsequent probability estimates an exhaustive list of possible discrepancy events. The events can overlap, so their probabilities are combined by a union bound.
feedback.advice: Keep the shared-data statement and the precise cell-block versus single-bit distinction.

locator.quote: since $J_i$ is uniform on the unqueried rows

feedback.feedback: The uniformity claim is valid before the first discovery of that column’s zero and for a newly queried row. As written, the preceding sentence speaks of a query with fewer than m/2 rows queried, which could include a repeated query to a zero already discovered.
feedback.why_it_matters: The proof counts discoveries, so the argument is repairable without changing the estimate, but the conditional-probability sentence is wider than its intended event.
feedback.advice: Make first discovery explicit and either remove repeat queries or state that they contribute no new discoveries. This is a local event-description repair.

locator.quote: A sharper count, which we cite from

feedback.feedback: The sharper constant is immediately declared unnecessary. Its appearance in the short proof invites a detour from the two-event argument to a refinement that changes neither exponent nor contradiction.
feedback.why_it_matters: It breaks the proof’s pace without strengthening the claim this paper is using.
feedback.advice: Keep the refinement in the record and, if desired, place its link in a final remark after the lower bound rather than inside the erased-zero estimate.

locator.quote: The position of a query already names an address:

feedback.feedback: This is the clearest sentence in the classical mechanism. It explains why even a query to a blank cell can be converted into a predictor, before any cell contents are read.
feedback.why_it_matters: It makes the simulation and direct-product application comprehensible to a reader coming from the quantum half.
feedback.advice: Keep the sentence before the simulator, and retain the explicit jointly independent free information.

locator.quote: Fix a column $i$ and a time $\tau

feedback.feedback: The simulator paragraph contains free information, emulation, a total-query cutoff, output convention, per-instance cap implication and event inclusion in one long block. The proof is correct in structure, but the inclusion that yields (12) is difficult to isolate.
feedback.why_it_matters: The reader can lose the single purpose of the construction: an un-aborted correct-cell query yields a correct answer vector.
feedback.advice: Separate the simulator definition from the event-inclusion argument. A short numbered procedure is justified here because it is an actual algorithm, followed by one sentence applying Lemma 4.

locator.quote: This bounds a joint event under the original law.

feedback.feedback: The joint-event formulation is precise, and the next sentence correctly explains why conditioning on being light is not a legitimate shortcut.
feedback.why_it_matters: It prevents adaptive query allocation from being mistaken for harmless conditioning of independent address instances.
feedback.advice: Preserve this distinction and its counterexample link, while allowing the details of the counterexample to remain outside the proof.

locator.quote: For the constant in (2), take $k\ge2$, $t\ge8$

feedback.feedback: The floor estimates are elementary and useful for the explicit constant, but they occupy the final paragraph of the classical argument immediately before another section of threshold arithmetic.
feedback.why_it_matters: The reader’s last impression of the lower bound is rounding rather than the planted-cell obstruction.
feedback.advice: End the mechanism with (15) and its interpretation. Put the floor calculation with the explicit-threshold material or in a short optional constants remark.

locator.quote: Theorem 1 uses only (5).

feedback.feedback: This sentence correctly identifies the minimal supplier, but the section then mixes that sufficient citation with a different uniform result, explicit threshold arithmetic and an outline of a new proof route.
feedback.why_it_matters: Readers cannot easily tell which material is needed for the fixed-k theorem and which supports quantitative refinements or the growing-k remark.
feedback.advice: Give the section two clear roles: the cited fixed-k ingredient used by the main proof, and the optional uniform refinement supplied by the record. Make the latter’s destination in §6 explicit.

locator.quote: by a stopped-martingale induction in the style of Girish, Tal and Wu

feedback.feedback: The proof outline names several substantial techniques without displaying the inequality that connects them. It is too detailed to function as a citation and too compressed to explain the argument.
feedback.why_it_matters: A quantum specialist cannot assess the new uniform estimate from this paragraph, but may infer that a complete proof was somehow sketched.
feedback.advice: Either keep a short description of the route and link directly to the record, or identify the existing two decisive bounds—an upper bound on shallow-tree distinguishing advantage and the lower advantage forced by an amplified solver. Do not add a compressed substitute for the full proof.

locator.quote: it is not the minimax law $\mu$ of §4

feedback.feedback: Distinguishing the Gaussian-chain law used to prove hardness from the promised minimax law used in the total-function lower bound is necessary and well placed.
feedback.why_it_matters: It prevents an off-promise distribution from silently entering the planted-address argument.
feedback.advice: Keep this explicit separation, even if the rest of the outline is shortened.

locator.quote: The quantifiers come in the order:

feedback.feedback: The fixed-exponent, fixed-k, then growing-m order is now clear, as is the distinction between excluding every smaller universal power and proving an exact quartic separation.
feedback.why_it_matters: This is the cleanest route from the family bounds to α_tot=4 and should remain the paper’s logical ending.
feedback.advice: Keep it, and align the exposition’s exercise about α_tot≥3.5 with this infimum argument rather than with exclusion of the bound at 3.5 itself.

locator.quote: \varepsilon(\ell)=8\sqrt{10/\ell}+(56\log_2\ell+508)/\ell

feedback.feedback: The explicit error exponent is more detailed than the role of this optional remark requires. Its large constants initially make the displayed lower bound uninformative, and a reader has to parse them to recover the simple statement that ε tends to zero.
feedback.why_it_matters: The clean optimal-power conclusion is followed by a bulky formula whose proof is elsewhere.
feedback.advice: State the qualitative uniform-family consequence and the chosen k(t), and leave the exact ε formula at the linked record derivation. If retaining the formula, say explicitly that the assertion is asymptotic and no useful finite-size ratio is being claimed at the initial threshold.

locator.quote: use only Lean's standard axioms

feedback.feedback: The formal section has removed the old hashes and review-status prose, which is an improvement. It still spends several paragraphs on axiom names, infimum nonemptiness, quantified circuit witnesses, two constants for the universal bound, and two amplification implementations.
feedback.why_it_matters: A specialist who wants to know what is formalised must sift through details of very different relevance, and the section risks regrowing the appendix that round six intentionally shortened.
feedback.advice: Keep the result, modelling convention, common-circuit scope and genuinely different lemma interfaces in concise mathematical prose. Leave axiom taxonomy, alternative constant routes and the full statement inventory at the linked record. Do not remove the measured/retained distinction just to save words.

locator.quote: a procedure that measures the label and resets its workspace

feedback.feedback: The measured/reset implementation is now distinguished from the separate retained-state result. That distinction is clear and addresses the exact claim the upper-bound sampler consumes.
feedback.why_it_matters: It avoids implying that formal equivalence of the two procedures has been proved merely because both fit an informal amplification story.
feedback.advice: Keep this wording and carry the same distinction into record §5.2; shorten surrounding detail rather than deleting the qualification.

locator.quote: under the author's direction.

feedback.feedback: The disclosure is brief and does not intrude into the proof or claim a human review that the packet does not establish.
feedback.why_it_matters: It informs the reader while leaving the mathematical argument as the reason to engage with the paper.
feedback.advice: Keep the disclosure short; do not add receipts, hashes or repeated epistemic warnings to the PDF.

locator.section: Appendix A, table caption and body references
locator.quote: Table 1 lists steps that are tempting to simplify

feedback.feedback: The body repeatedly refers to numbered rows, but the rendered table has no row numbers. Readers must count long wrapped rows to find row 7, and the zero-query cap examples use a different parameter regime from the eventual construction.
feedback.why_it_matters: A well-designed set of counterexamples becomes unnecessarily awkward to navigate.
feedback.advice: Add small row labels or descriptive cross-reference names, and state that the toy cap examples test the general lemma hypotheses, not the final construction’s large-parameter regime.

locator.quote: yet no column wins

feedback.feedback: The false-dominant example relies on every other column containing a zero and on column 1 being smallest in the tie-break order. The latter is visible; the former is only implicit in the phrase correct certificate except one pointer.
feedback.why_it_matters: Readers should be able to verify the counterexample without supplying unstated board conditions.
