locator.quote: We always have $Q\leq1-\varepsilon$, even when $Q$ is negative.

feedback.feedback: The signed-estimate check is worth preserving. Multiplying an inductive lower bound by a success probability and then subtracting a failure penalty is a place where a handwave can reverse the needed inequality. The proof explicitly handles the negative case instead of assuming the lower estimate is a probability.
feedback.why_it_matters: This small paragraph supplies the exact justification a referee needs for the continuation induction.
feedback.advice: Keep the argument, with the local scalar renamed as suggested separately. It is an example of useful detail rather than routine constant arithmetic.

locator.quote: We now choose $k=\lfloor\sqrt{t/20}\rfloor$

feedback.feedback: The choice is motivated only after a long expansion of C_k and another floor calculation. The illuminating tradeoff appears later as 40k+ell/k: increasing k reduces the classical exponent deficit but increases the quantum decoder overhead. That balance explains the square-root schedule.
feedback.why_it_matters: The reader initially receives a parameter choice as a numerical trick rather than a consequence of the two costs competing.
feedback.advice: Preview the competing terms before expanding the constant, then retain the exact derivation that validates the existing schedule. This would explain the present result without proposing a different schedule or stronger theorem.

locator.quote: The chain gives the constant $474$; we state $508$, the value used in the specialist companion.

feedback.feedback: This sentence explains an editorial reconciliation rather than a mathematical necessity. The proof legitimately relaxes one constant to another, but saying it does so because another document already uses that number makes the derivation sound driven by synchronization with a draft.
feedback.why_it_matters: It draws attention away from the actual conservative inequality and makes the reader wonder whether the constants were chosen independently of the proof.
feedback.advice: Describe 508 simply as a convenient common upper bound, with any cross-document reconciliation retained in revision notes. Keep all three documents on the same stated bound.

locator.quote: The prefactor can be checked on two bits.

feedback.feedback: The sensitivity matrix, its masks and the progress drop are useful new parts of this check. The complete one-query parity-state derivation is already given in §2.6, however, and is repeated here before the genuinely relevant matrix calculation.
feedback.why_it_matters: The appendix makes a careful diagnostic feel longer than its new mathematical content requires.
feedback.advice: Refer back to the exact parity algorithm in §2.6 and keep the explicit adversary matrix, eigenvalues and progress drop here. The source-prefactor comparison remains recoverable without repeating the entire preparation.

locator.quote: A separate older annex transcription inserted an extra square root around the entire denominator.

feedback.feedback: The distinction between an error in an earlier annex transcription and the printed source discrepancy is useful provenance, but it interrupts the mathematical witness. A first-time reader has not seen that older annex and does not need its correction history to understand the factor-two issue.
feedback.why_it_matters: A clear exact example turns into a report about the project’s earlier debugging session.
feedback.advice: Keep the edition-specific claim, exact counterexample and limit of the conclusion in Appendix A. Move the older-transcription chronology to execution/source-comparison notes rather than expanding it in the proof.

locator.quote: Pre-success state: m^{-1/2} sum_{i=1}^m |i> tensor_{b=1}^t |phi(i,p_b)>.

feedback.feedback: The catalogue’s mathematical content is useful, but its ASCII-style expressions and raw claim-name headings are much harder to read than the surrounding typeset record. A reader who follows a mathematical claim into the catalogue encounters a serialization format rather than a concise mathematical statement.
feedback.why_it_matters: The catalogue is intended to reduce recovery cost, but the notation translation becomes an extra step before following its proof links.
feedback.advice: Give entries readable mathematical titles and rendered notation while retaining their exact IDs as anchors. Preserve the machine-readable catalogue separately if it is needed by tooling.

locator.quote: [§5.2](#upper-continuation-induction)

feedback.feedback: The anchor resolves to the continuation induction, but that passage is now in §5.5. The same stale visible label appears in the catalogue’s claim-error entry. The link technically works, which is why checking only anchor existence misses the defect.
feedback.why_it_matters: A reader switching between printed sections and hyperlinks is told two different locations for the same argument.
feedback.advice: Update the displayed section labels from the current heading tree and check the other catalogue links semantically. This is separate from the stale companion-section references near the record’s beginning.

locator.quote: This account is written for a graduate student who knows the query models above

feedback.feedback: The paragraph now honestly declares substantial prerequisites, but it answers the previous review by narrowing the audience. The packet asks for a mathematician from another field or a strong undergraduate who has not studied query complexity. Knowing the oracle models, unknown-probability amplification, uncomputation, Yao and adaptive decision-tree conditioning is already a substantial quantum-query course. This is a scope mismatch, not a request to delete the useful prerequisite disclosure.
feedback.why_it_matters: The intended newcomer can be excluded before the first example, even though the main construction can be taught with several of these results stated as precise tools.
feedback.advice: Keep the reader promised by the assignment. Teach the few operations actually used, and state the deeper results as inputs with their contracts. Keep the more demanding route available as a quantum-course reading route. The existing exposition skill explicitly forbids treating stronger prerequisites as completion of a fixed-audience task.

locator.quote: A quantum algorithm reads through the oracle $O_x|j,b,w\rangle=|j,b\oplus x_j,w\rangle$

feedback.feedback: The model arrives as a ket transformation in the third sentence, before the reader is told what a register or an oracle call is. Saying that it acts on a superposition can easily suggest that one query returns a readable list of all input bits. The text also leaves the distinction between a query and an ordinary computational gate implicit.
feedback.why_it_matters: Every later cheap quantum step depends on counting oracle invocations, not on getting all the bit values for free.
feedback.advice: At first use, identify j as an address, b as a one-bit answer register, and w as temporary memory; say that one invocation counts as one query and that measuring the resulting state does not reveal all x_j. State that input-independent computation is not charged. A short four-position state example would do more than additional general quantum prose.

locator.quote: some constant }C\text{ gives }R(f)\le C\,(1+Q(f))^{\alpha}

feedback.feedback: The displayed infimum is correct, but its most consequential quantifier is left to the notation: C must work for every total function and every input length. A reader may confuse that universal C with the k-dependent C_k in the very next display, or think the theorem compares two algorithms for one fixed input length.
feedback.why_it_matters: Without the universal scope, choosing a constant after seeing a function makes the optimal-exponent question trivial.
feedback.advice: Give the quantifier one ordinary sentence before the display: the same multiplicative constant must work throughout the class. Then explicitly separate it from constants attached to a fixed construction parameter. Explain the harmless 1+Q convention only if needed to avoid a question about Q=0.

locator.quote: R\approx m^{2-1/k}=(\sqrt m)^{4-2/k}\approx Q^{4-2/k}

feedback.feedback: The approximation chain is visually stronger than the established claims. The argument supplies an upper bound on Q and a lower bound on R; it does not establish that either displayed algorithm is optimal for this particular family. The use of approximately equal signs suppresses both logarithms and the direction of the inequalities.
feedback.why_it_matters: A newcomer may leave believing an exact relationship or matching family bounds have been proved, rather than a separation sufficient to exclude smaller universal powers.
feedback.advice: Preserve the one-line arithmetic, but label it explicitly as comparing the proved lower and upper scales. Use directional language or inequalities when moving from those scales to R versus Q. The final ratio argument already has the correct logic.

locator.section: Introduction: theorem before a numerical foothold
locator.quote: A single $k$ reaches only the exponent $4-2/k$

feedback.feedback: The first two pages contain k, m, L, r and an infimum but no concrete exponent value. The later k=3 example comes only in Section 6. A new reader is asked to feel why this is an advance over quadratic and cubic separation before seeing one instance of the arithmetic.
feedback.why_it_matters: The title promises an explanation of four, while the opening can look like a collection of unrelated parameters.
feedback.advice: At this first occurrence, use one existing specialization, such as fixed k=3 giving exponent 10/3 up to the displayed losses, and then point out what increases as k increases. This is substitution into the stated bounds, not an additional result.

locator.quote: a certificate that $F=1$ sits in one of them

feedback.feedback: Certificate is doing substantial work before it has a definition. In query complexity it is a set of revealed input bits forcing an answer, while the later cell stores proposed circuit values and pointers that still require checking. A student may read the cell itself as an externally trusted proof.
feedback.why_it_matters: The construction relies on distinguishing stored claims from a verified winning certificate, especially on malformed inputs.
feedback.advice: Define a certificate in one elementary example or a parenthetical sentence, then call a cell a proposed certificate until its local tests pass. Keep the distinction between input data and proof of its correctness consistent through the column construction.

locator.quote: Tal reached $8/3-o(1)$

feedback.feedback: The history lists 5/2, 8/3 and 3, but only the final cubic ceiling receives a mechanism. Tal appears as a number in a chronology. A quantum reader wants to know whether each gain came from a better partial-function separation, a different totalization, or a different evaluation algorithm.
feedback.why_it_matters: The sequence can be memorized without understanding which bottleneck the present tournament removes.
feedback.advice: Either compress the intermediate numerical history and link to the companion, or attach one concrete role to each retained milestone. Keep the detailed old-route-versus-new-route arithmetic, which is the part that teaches something.

locator.quote: The cheat-sheet function composes a partial function $g$ on $n$ bits with AND-OR

feedback.feedback: Composition has a direction, and n is used both for the logical input size of g and for the side length of a gadget. A newcomer cannot tell from this sentence whether g replaces each AND-OR bit or AND-OR replaces each input bit of g. The subsequent product n^2 R(g) assumes the latter construction.
feedback.why_it_matters: The cubic-ceiling calculation is one of the best ideas in the exposition, but its scaling is difficult to reconstruct from the prose alone.
feedback.advice: Say which logical bits are replaced by which gadgets, and identify the gadget input count separately from the logical input count. A small block-of-blocks sketch or the notation g composed with AND-OR would settle the direction before the cost multiplication.

locator.quote: Section 1 computes $k$-fold Forrelation on three eight-bit inputs

feedback.feedback: The first concrete matrix begins on PDF page 3, after nearly two pages of model definitions, an infimum, exact constants, construction overview, milestone history, an AND-OR comparison, prerequisites and a full route map. The examples-first title is therefore asking the reader to wait through a specialist-style introduction before its main teaching device begins.
feedback.why_it_matters: The opening demands more working memory than the small example would require and risks losing exactly the intended non-specialist reader.
feedback.advice: Keep the question, the directional exponent arithmetic and a short route map at the entrance. Move the long historical comparison to the point where the failed direct search is explained, or offer it as a marked side route. This is an ordering recommendation, not a request to remove the theorem from page one.

locator.quote: apply the signs $z_2$ with one query

feedback.feedback: This is the first consequential use of phase kickback, but the opening oracle writes x_j into an answer bit. The missing bridge is exactly how that bit-query oracle multiplies an address amplitude by (-1)^{x_j} while retaining the address. Calling it phase kickback in Section 3 arrives after the reader has already needed it.
feedback.why_it_matters: The two-query claim can look like a new, more powerful oracle than the one defined at the beginning.
feedback.advice: Give the one-line action on an answer qubit prepared in the minus state, and explain that the answer register factors back out. Also say that the Walsh transform and projection are input-independent operations, hence cost no input queries.

locator.quote: so a single run happens to decide them

feedback.feedback: Them grammatically refers to all three inputs, although a^- has no value under P and the experiment treats it exactly like a^+. The next paragraph corrects the reader, but this sentence briefly announces a decision that has not been defined.
feedback.why_it_matters: The distinction between an accepted measurement outcome and a correct answer to the partial function is the lesson of the example.
feedback.advice: Scope the sentence to the two promised examples, and describe the third as an accepted unpromised input. Retain the subsequent one-input with acceptance probability 1/4; it successfully prevents the examples from making the general decoder look exact.

locator.quote: and project onto $u$

feedback.feedback: Projection is introduced as a verb without an operational interpretation. A mathematically literate reader may understand orthogonal projection of a vector but not that this is a two-outcome quantum measurement, with a success branch and its complementary branch.
feedback.why_it_matters: The later sampler reuses success flags and conditioning on measurement; this is the earliest place to teach that operation concretely.
feedback.advice: Identify the two possible measurement outcomes and derive the success probability as the squared inner product with u. For this small Walsh system, mention the equivalent inverse-Walsh-and-zero-outcome test if that is the representation the author wants to carry forward.

locator.quote: Of all $256$ inputs, $104$ are one-inputs, $48$ are zero-inputs and $104$ lie outside the promise

feedback.feedback: The full census is exact but has no later use. It occurs immediately after the key quantum lesson, and the reader must decide whether these proportions matter to the hard distribution or to the acceptance algorithm. They do not: the later minimax distribution is a different object.
feedback.why_it_matters: An unrelated count can look like evidence for an asymptotic lower bound that the next sentence correctly says this example cannot illustrate.
feedback.advice: Put the census in the linked checking script or offer it as an optional exercise. Keep the L=0 limitation and the promise-versus-projection lesson in the main text.

locator.quote: We describe one column in general, then a four-column board.

feedback.feedback: The section postpones the concrete column until after three input families, an addressed array, four winning conditions and two attribution paragraphs. At this stage the reader has only seen two sign vectors, not a circuit transcript or a pointer array.
feedback.why_it_matters: The schema is easier to remember once the reader has watched one actual address select one actual cell.
feedback.advice: Consider introducing the four-column layout first with only the fields needed to identify its winner, then name the general fields. Preserve the explicit statement that r=2 is a teaching simplification, which is already a successful repair from the previous round.

locator.quote: Column $i$ **wins** at address $s$ when four conditions hold

feedback.feedback: The four clauses are compressed into one semicolon-separated paragraph, yet later passages refer to individual clauses and the Lean section asks the reader to inspect the second one. The clause structure is conceptually important but difficult to scan.
feedback.why_it_matters: Readers cannot quickly compare a changed board against the definition or check that the local-test list covers every obligation.
feedback.advice: Present the four genuinely parallel conditions as numbered clauses or a compact table, with the corresponding test family beside each. Keep the explanation of uniqueness immediately after them; it should not be separated from the pointer condition.

locator.quote: each reading one proposed gate value and the two values feeding it

feedback.feedback: The previous-round plan SX-014 called for a pointer test and a gate test with their actual bit reads. The pointer test is now worked, but the gate test is still only described abstractly. All stored transcripts in the board are correct, so the reader never sees the local consistency check detect a false transcript.
feedback.why_it_matters: The reason an arbitrary input can carry a useful certificate without trusting it remains asserted rather than demonstrated.
feedback.advice: Use one existing gate from the linked 180-gate circuit, show its two predecessor values and proposed output, and flip only that output to show exactly which local equation fails. Keep the example tiny and use it to explain why a transcript is input data, not an oracle for circuit evaluation.

locator.quote: Shannon expansion of the truth tables gives such a circuit with $180$ gates

feedback.feedback: Shannon expansion and the exact count 180 enter together without an explanation of either. The relevant point here is that a fixed public circuit exists and that a stored evaluation can be checked locally. The precise gate count is useful only for the later K=371 illustration.
feedback.why_it_matters: The named construction sounds like an additional prerequisite at the point where the reader is learning the certificate mechanism.
feedback.advice: Define the truth-table expansion in a short phrase if retained, or move its name to the linked circuit file. Make the role of 180 explicit: it supplies a concrete test count, not a new conceptual ingredient.

locator.quote: that cell certifies the answers

feedback.feedback: The general-column picture emphasizes certifying address bits but does not visibly distinguish the domain checks from the value checks. The domain-bit counterexample immediately following the figure is one of the document’s central points.
feedback.why_it_matters: A reader who recalls the diagram instead of the paragraph may remember only address agreement, precisely the insufficient condition the changed board refutes.
feedback.advice: Add the domain-and-value distinction inside the cell’s short label or caption. The figure need not show the entire circuit; it should name the two kinds of conclusion its transcripts certify.

locator.quote: Column $1$ wins at $10$ (Figure 2); every other column has a zero in its own string, so $F=1$.

feedback.feedback: The final so appears to make the zeros in the other columns the reason F=1. Those zeros show that the other columns cannot win; the positive value follows from column 1 satisfying all four conditions.
feedback.why_it_matters: This is a small causal slip at the first complete evaluation of the new function.
feedback.advice: Separate the positive conclusion from the uniqueness observation: first identify why column 1 passes, then use the zeros to exclude the others.

locator.quote: On the changed board, $(2,00)$ fails only its domain test

feedback.feedback: This is an excellent exact instance of a single bad local test, but the exposition does not carry it into the quantum verifier later. With K=371, one uniform local test detects the error with probability 1/371; that is exactly why the verification uses amplitude amplification.
feedback.why_it_matters: The circuit examples and the quantum subroutine remain separate lessons when they could explain one another.
feedback.advice: Recall this same candidate in the Verification paragraph and use its one failing test to connect the stored-domain mistake to the threshold 1/K. Keep the exact Grover iteration calculation optional; the detection probability is the decisive bridge.

locator.quote: which of column $2$'s tests fail at each of its four addresses?

feedback.feedback: This question tests a real distinction: a correct transcript can still fail the domain requirement, while an address mismatch contributes additional value-test failures. The answer is separate and can be checked directly from the data on the page.
feedback.why_it_matters: It gives the reader an independent task tied to the actual total-function definition, rather than asking for a paraphrase of a theorem.
feedback.advice: Keep it next to the changed board. If the four winning clauses are numbered, use the same numbering in the answer.

locator.quote: let $W_{ab}=(-1)^{a\cdot b}$, $H=W/\sqrt m$

feedback.feedback: The dot product in the exponent is not specified as a binary dot product, and the text immediately uses H as a length-preserving operator. The four-by-four example verifies this once, but the general formula asks the reader to supply the Walsh orthogonality argument.
feedback.why_it_matters: The norm bound on Phi and the legality of the quantum experiment both depend on this normalization.
feedback.advice: Say that the exponent is computed modulo two, and identify H as the tensor product of the normalized two-by-two Hadamard transform. That supplies the relevant general fact without a separate proof excursion.

locator.quote: Repeating it $\rho=\lceil16c^{-1}\ln(1/\eta)\rceil$ times

feedback.feedback: The parameter eta is first introduced inside the trial-count formula. The companion supplies the range 0<eta<1/2; the exposition does not name eta as the requested error tolerance before using it.
feedback.why_it_matters: Later eta, epsilon and epsilon/r appear at different levels, and the reader needs their roles rather than three unexplained small quantities.
feedback.advice: State the requested decoder error range before the formula, then name the later specialization eta=epsilon/r when decoding an address. Keep the distinction between per-bit error and per-address error explicit.

locator.quote: decides $P$ with error at most $\eta$

feedback.feedback: The sentence ends with a query bound on every input, but correctness holds only on the promise. These are intentionally different scopes. Section 4 relies on the total running-time guarantee even for unpromised losers, while final verification handles the lack of a correct P-value there.
feedback.why_it_matters: This split is the central obstacle in turning the partial function into a total one; it is too easy to lose inside a long sentence.
feedback.advice: End the decoder paragraph by putting the two guarantees side by side in ordinary language: correctness on promised inputs; the same finite query cap on all inputs. This reinforces an existing argument rather than adding a warning or a new assumption.

locator.quote: Because $\Phi$ has two boundary factors and $k-1$ internal factors of $m^{-1/2}$

feedback.feedback: The integer numerator, two threshold comparisons, ripple-carry arithmetic and the constant 200 receive one dense paragraph, but the reason the reader needs a nearly linear circuit is deferred. For this audience, the supplier’s role matters before its implementation details.
feedback.why_it_matters: The reader can spend effort parsing arithmetic that never becomes an operation they perform, while missing why S controls the final quantum cost.
feedback.advice: Lead with the consumed fact S=O_k(m log^2 m) and its consequence for the number of local tests. Put the exact integer derivation in an optional calculation or direct the reader to the existing record proof.

locator.quote: two boundary factors

feedback.feedback: Boundary refers to the two u vectors, not to a boundary case of the promise. This terminology is never explained, and the following denominator 2^{t(k+1)} is the first expression that depends on counting those normalizations.
feedback.why_it_matters: An elementary normalization count becomes harder to reconstruct than the displayed product itself.
feedback.advice: If the integer calculation remains on the main route, identify the two u factors and the k−1 copies of H explicitly. This is a local naming repair, distinct from the recommendation about how much circuit arithmetic to retain.

locator.quote: which is $O_k(m^{22}(\log m)^3)$

feedback.feedback: The large input length is presented as a formula and then immediately left behind. A reader may confuse m with the number of input bits or interpret the quartic separation as a running-time result in the full input length.
feedback.why_it_matters: The comparison between R and Q is meaningful even though the addressed array is large, but the meaning of the complexity parameter must remain clear.
feedback.advice: Attach one sentence distinguishing m from the total bit count n and explaining that the theorem compares the two query measures for the same large input family. Avoid suggesting practical end-to-end speedups from the query exponent alone.

locator.quote: The construction uses $k$-fold Forrelation through three facts

feedback.feedback: This is the right abstraction boundary: low quantum cost, a small exact circuit, and classical hardness have different jobs. A reader can understand the total-function construction without reproducing the full Forrelation lower bound.
feedback.why_it_matters: Keeping those jobs separate prevents the promise-solving algorithm from being mistaken for an exact domain checker.
feedback.advice: Preserve the three-part interface. Add the downstream job to each label if revising the paragraph order: decode, verify, and force classical work.

locator.quote: Checking that one column wins means reading its $m$ string bits and following its $m-1$ pointers

feedback.feedback: The sentence describes reading m bits and following m−1 pointers, then assigns that operation about sqrt(m) quantum queries. That is not what literally reading all those bits costs. The intended operation is bounded-error search for a violation among the local tests.
feedback.why_it_matters: The first explanation of the quantum speedup can accidentally teach that a quantum algorithm reads a whole classical string in sqrt(m) queries.
feedback.advice: Name the violation-search operation explicitly. Include transcript and output tests in the reference to K, then suppress logarithms for the intuitive sqrt(m) comparison. Preserve the useful warning that nesting this verification inside Grover over columns would lose the desired exponent.

locator.section: §4: nested search and the new mechanism
locator.quote: run the expensive check only on a short list of candidates

feedback.feedback: This is the mechanism that turns the upper bound from roughly m into roughly sqrt(m), but the paragraph does not give the reader a compact view of the complete algorithm before the weight analysis starts. It is easy to mistake all the later weight updates for operations the computer executes.
feedback.why_it_matters: The novel sampler is easier to assess when the operational stages are known in advance.
feedback.advice: Give a short procedural outline: initialize the candidate list; use the coherent comparison preparation to sample another pivot; stop at a cap or reported failure; verify the accumulated candidates. Keep the ideal weights in a visibly separate analysis paragraph, as the text already says they are not computed.

locator.quote: Then we follow each decoded cell's pointer into the other column

feedback.feedback: The pointer test in Section 2 reads one direction. The first comparison needs both directions, two decoded labels, a disqualification rule and a tie rule, but no full comparison is traced before the general probabilities a_ij are introduced.
feedback.why_it_matters: The reader must mentally compose several earlier operations and can easily reverse which column a zero disqualifies.
feedback.advice: Trace the existing pair 1 versus 2, showing the label returned for the unpromised a^- input, both pointer destinations, and the resulting victor. Make clear that the returned label in column 2 is not its true partial-function address.

locator.quote: Both orders of a pair run the same procedure

feedback.feedback: The companion explicitly sorts the two indices and runs one circuit for the unordered pair. Here same procedure could be read as two ordered calls whose roles or tie decisions are separately defined. The complement identity needs one common experiment with opposite outcome labels.
feedback.why_it_matters: The exact identity a_ij+a_ji=1 is the entire drift argument’s algebraic input.
feedback.advice: Retain the companion’s short implementation convention: normalize the unordered pair once and interpret the one outcome in the requested order. There is no need to add circuit machinery.

locator.section: §4: coherent implementation of the repeated decoder
locator.quote: Its trials, counts and decoded labels stay unmeasured in workspace

feedback.feedback: Section 1 explicitly described a projection measurement and Section 3 repeated that experiment. This sentence now says those trials remain unmeasured. A newcomer needs the bridge from a measured probability calculation to a reversible circuit that records outcome bits without measuring them.
feedback.why_it_matters: Otherwise the inverse used by amplitude amplification appears to undo a physical measurement, which it cannot do.
feedback.advice: Explain that each would-be measurement result is retained in a flag register, the count and threshold are computed reversibly, and actual measurement is postponed. Keep the workspace through the inverse; do not describe it as already cleaned at this point.

locator.quote: and this is what makes $a_{ij}$ well defined

feedback.feedback: The probability a_ij is well defined for any specified comparison measurement. Retaining labels establishes the stronger and relevant statement that the coherent comparison has the same output law as the decoded-label rule. The current ending understates that correspondence and suggests a definitional problem instead.
feedback.why_it_matters: The reader should see why coherence preserves the specific probabilities used in the classical weight analysis.
feedback.advice: End at equality of the two output laws. Preserve the explanation that orthogonal label branches contribute probabilities without cross terms.

locator.quote: Quantum minimum finding [@DH1996] needs a total order

feedback.feedback: The quantum-side comparison jumps from minimum finding and bounded-error search directly to the present algorithm. The packet’s two 2026 comparison-based separations and king-finding paper appear in the bibliography but are never used in the exposition’s body. The companion identifies a more immediate set-to-weight relationship.
feedback.why_it_matters: The reader may infer that comparison-based candidate generation followed by verification is itself the new contribution, rather than the treatment of arbitrarily biased loser comparisons.
feedback.advice: Add a short, audience-appropriate comparison to the existing candidate-set and exact-orientation approaches, then identify the new fractional probabilities. Keep the distinction between certificate-complexity separation and randomized-query separation; do not import their theorems as if they already prove this result.

locator.quote: column $4$'s pointer into column $3$ names position $1$

feedback.feedback: The three modified pointers are supplied in one long sentence, while the drawn edge labels mix the modified pointers with the unmodified pointers that actually certify each victory. The figure is correct, but checking one edge requires recovering both relevant pointer values from two sections.
feedback.why_it_matters: The example intended to make nontransitivity immediate still demands bookkeeping before the cycle is visible.
feedback.advice: Give a compact three-row comparison table listing the two target bits and the winner, or explicitly trace one edge and let the diagram carry the remaining two. Keep the current arrow convention and the fact that every cell is changed together.

locator.quote: so the decoders are exact and the comparisons deterministic

feedback.feedback: The worked sampler deliberately makes every comparison deterministic. Consequently every weight is 0 or 1 and sampling by weight is just uniform sampling from surviving candidates. This illustrates cyclicity and measurement, but it never exhibits the fractional-weight feature that distinguishes the algorithm from set pruning. The previous round moved the fractional example out; the next-layer problem is that the surviving example no longer witnesses the novelty.
feedback.why_it_matters: A reader can successfully run every exercise and still not understand why weights, exact conditional output laws and no margin from 1/2 matter.
feedback.advice: Start from the existing abstract four-candidate example in record §5.2, which already gives unequal weights. To expose the arbitrary-loser feature as well, change one loser pair to a_ab=a_ba=1/2: after pivot a, the weights are (1−eps,0,1/2,1). Show their sum, success mass equal to that sum divided by four, and conditional pivot probabilities proportional to them. Label this as an abstract comparison-matrix variation, not an asserted realization by the addressed four-column board. No new theorem or bound is needed.

locator.quote: pairing the terms $w_iw_pa_{ip}$ and $w_pw_ia_{pi}$

feedback.feedback: The pairing is the decisive elementary move, but the next display jumps directly to the full double sum. On a first reading it is easy to miss that the two pivot probabilities are already weighted, or that the diagonal terms vanish.
feedback.why_it_matters: The elegant reason for the halving bound gets hidden behind notation even though it can be demonstrated in one pair.
feedback.advice: Write one pair’s contribution as w_i w_p(a_ip+a_pi)=w_i w_p and explicitly remove i=p using a_ii=0. Then give the displayed full identity. Preserve the initial four-pivot table, which provides a useful numerical check.

locator.quote: Meanwhile the winner's weight stays at least $(1-\varepsilon)^T

feedback.feedback: The preceding paragraph bounds expected total weight, while this one bounds the winner’s weight on each history before selection. That change in logical strength is essential to the missing-winner event inclusion but is not named.
feedback.why_it_matters: A student may think both statements are expectations and fail to see why a small expected total forces the winner to have been selected.
feedback.advice: Say that the lower bound holds on every unselected-winner history, then connect that pathwise fact to the expectation bound. The current Markov calculation can remain unchanged.

locator.quote: Suppose pivots $p_1,\dots,p_j$ have been chosen.

feedback.feedback: The preparation is described only with an existing pivot list. The initial empty-history case is what starts the actual algorithm and makes the ideal first-pivot table relevant, but its empty-product convention is never stated.
feedback.why_it_matters: The process can appear to require a pivot before it knows how to obtain one.
feedback.advice: Add that with no previous pivots every branch has success flag 1 and the first measured pivot is uniform over columns. It requires no comparisons. This is a useful operational base case, not a new analysis.

locator.section: §4: good state at zero success probability
locator.quote: let $g$ be the normalised state on its success branch

feedback.feedback: This definition needs p>0, while the same paragraph later emphasizes the p=0 case. The expert lemma correctly limits the normalized successful state to p>0. There is no normalized success branch at p=0.
feedback.why_it_matters: The exposition’s most important all-input endpoint is being described with an object undefined there.
feedback.advice: Copy the short p>0 qualification from the companion, and handle p=0 separately through certain failure. This is a statement clarification, not a gap in the intended bounded-amplification argument.

locator.quote: the state is exactly $g$, whatever the number of iterations

feedback.feedback: The successful amplitude sin((2j+1)theta) can be negative, so the normalized vector can be -g. The companion correctly says up to a global phase. The measurable conclusion needed here, preservation of the conditional column distribution, is unaffected.
feedback.why_it_matters: The word exactly creates an unnecessary discrepancy between the two funnel documents at the place where state versus output-law distinctions matter.
feedback.advice: Use the companion’s global-phase qualification or state only the invariant conditional label law. Do not expand the exposition into a discussion of formal vector representatives.

locator.section: §4: standard amplification proof dominates the route
locator.quote: Either way a trial succeeds with probability at least $9/40$.

feedback.feedback: The current paragraph retains M=ceil(10/sqrt(gamma)), the 3/4 case split, 19/40, 9/40 and ln(40/31). Round-six SX-022, QX-020 and CX024 explicitly planned to move this recipe to the record while retaining the interface. The delivered paragraph is still a full unboxed standard proof, occupying the bottom of page 8 and spilling onto page 9.
feedback.why_it_matters: The newcomer must absorb constant-level amplification arithmetic immediately before the construction-specific sampler example, while the genuinely new fractional behavior has been removed.
feedback.advice: Implement the already accepted weighting decision: keep the fixed cap, unknown-p guarantee, certain failure at p=0 and preservation of the successful label distribution. Route the trial recipe and constants to record §5.1 or a clearly optional box.

locator.section: §4: coupling without a new probability prerequisite
locator.quote: Coupling the real and ideal processes until the first failure

feedback.feedback: Coupling is used as a technical verb without being defined. The preceding exact conditional law makes a very short explanation possible: as long as the histories agree and the real sampler succeeds, use the same pivot in both processes.
feedback.why_it_matters: The reader may treat the T epsilon term as a mysterious theorem or assume it requires independent stage failures.
feedback.advice: Give that common-pivot construction in a sentence and state that the per-history failure bound is enough for the union bound. Preserve the existing restriction to stages before the winner is listed.

locator.quote: Decoding errors inside comparisons are already part of the $a_{ij}$.

feedback.feedback: This short closing sentence explains why the analysis does not charge a decoder error for every one of the many coherent comparison calls. That is a major conceptual difference from a naive replacement of noisy comparisons by a perfect orientation, but it appears only after the full error budget.
feedback.why_it_matters: A quantum-trained reader may incorrectly expect the decoder accuracy to scale inversely with all amplified oracle uses and misunderstand the reason the tournament works.
feedback.advice: Promote this explanation to the point where a_ij is introduced or where the sampler is amplified. Explain that amplitude amplification manipulates the actual coherent comparison, whose output probabilities define the weights; the analysis never posits a globally correct hidden tournament.

locator.quote: amplify over the $K$ local tests

feedback.feedback: The local tests were described as adaptive classical bit reads, including following a pointer. The verifier now uses them in a coherent search without stating the implementation bridge that the companion supplies: a reversible controlled test-index evaluator and its inverse.
feedback.why_it_matters: The reader can wonder whether following all possible pointers in superposition assumes an extra memory-access primitive or makes the cost exponential in the array size.
feedback.advice: Explain that a local test computes its next bit address reversibly, uses the same bit oracle, and retains enough workspace to invert the computation, with a constant-factor query overhead. Link to the existing coherent-test argument for details.

locator.section: §4: actual query counts versus fixed caps
locator.quote: Every number of trials, iterations, stages and comparisons is fixed in advance

feedback.feedback: This is false as a description of the algorithm just given. A trial randomly chooses its number of Grover iterations; the amplification procedure stops at its first success; the tournament stops on reported failure; and a stage uses the number of pivots already obtained. The actual counts therefore vary between branches. The proof needs and has fixed upper bounds on those counts, not fixed realized counts.
feedback.why_it_matters: The sentence conflates a bounded adaptive algorithm with a fixed-length execution and weakens the explanation of the worst-case query convention.
feedback.advice: Replace the claim about fixed numbers by a claim about input-independent caps on every branch. Preserve early stopping and randomized iteration counts. The asymptotic upper bound does not need to change. The preprint §3.2 already uses fixed upper bounds rather than fixed realized counts; align this sentence with it.

locator.quote: A comparison costs $c=O_k(r\log(r/\varepsilon))$ queries

feedback.feedback: The symbol c previously meant the small probability delta^2 in Section 3; here it becomes a growing query cost. Neither use is wrong locally, but both reappear in the amplitude-amplification discussion and the reader is not told that the symbol has been repurposed.
feedback.why_it_matters: A reader checking the cost chain can inadvertently carry the probability c into the comparison-count formula.
feedback.advice: Use a descriptive cost symbol or state the cost without assigning c in the exposition. The companion may retain its compact specialist notation.

locator.quote: This is the $\sqrt m$ half of the arithmetic in the introduction.

feedback.feedback: The section returns to the exact quantity that motivated it, after distinguishing candidate generation from expensive verification. This closure is useful: it tells the reader which part of the theorem has now been supplied.
feedback.why_it_matters: A long algorithmic derivation otherwise risks losing the global separation argument.
feedback.advice: Keep this closing connection. If the standard amplification constants move out, use the recovered space to explain the fractional sampler rather than to expand the query-count algebra.

locator.quote: and leave every cell blank

feedback.feedback: Blank is an evocative diagram label, but the input was defined as an assignment of Boolean bits. The companion specifies that every cell bit is zero. Here blank can sound like absent data or a special symbol outside the input alphabet.
feedback.why_it_matters: The simulator must answer every queried cell bit, and its answer is what makes the dummy transcript independent of the planted column.
feedback.advice: Say once that blank means all bits are zero. Keep the visual blank-cell notation after that definition.

locator.section: §5: what the small example cannot prove
locator.quote: At $m=4$ there is no hard distribution

feedback.feedback: As written this is too strong. Section 1 gives L_{2,4}=0. A distribution assigning probability 1/2 each to the promised inputs a^+ and a^0 makes every zero-query algorithm correct with probability at most 1/2, hence meets the displayed at-most-2/3 hardness condition at this L. What fails at m=4 is a useful positive query budget and the later division by L, not the existence of any hard distribution.
feedback.why_it_matters: The caveat intended to prevent overclaiming introduces a false mathematical statement and obscures exactly which hypothesis the teaching board lacks.
feedback.advice: Say that the asymptotic hardness bound supplies no positive L at this size, so the picture illustrates the two places where inputs differ only. Retain the explicit reset of address inputs and cell contents introduced in the last revision. This is a local caveat correction; the main asymptotic theorem is unaffected.

locator.quote: condition on the whole transcript of the dummy run

feedback.feedback: The query-by-query discovery probability must be conditioned on the history so far, before the next query. Whole transcript can mean the completed run, which can already reveal whether a particular discovery occurred. The companion says given the past. The round-six repair correctly added independence of the other fields but left this temporal ambiguity.
feedback.why_it_matters: The same adaptive-conditioning discipline is used again in the direct-product proof, so a loose statement here teaches the wrong filtration.
feedback.advice: Say the entire observed history up to the current query, together with the fact that the current column’s zero has not yet been found. Then give the residual uniformity and 2/m bound. Do not claim the next discovery remains random after conditioning on its future answer.

locator.section: §5: why the classical gap is at least one third
locator.quote: A randomized algorithm computing $F$ with $G$ queries would have gap at least $1/3$

feedback.feedback: The concluding discrepancy contradiction is compact enough that the reader has to reconstruct the direction of both error inequalities. The construction of the pair is explicit, but the final link back to the definition of R is not written.
feedback.why_it_matters: This is where the lower-bound argument becomes a statement about every bounded-error algorithm, rather than only the selected dummy and planted distributions.
feedback.advice: Write the two inequalities for acceptance on Y^1 and Y^0, namely at least 2/3 and at most 1/3, before subtracting. The subsequent averaging over deterministic trees then has a visible target.

locator.section: §5: explaining the simulator as an address predictor
locator.quote: outputs $s$, read off from the position of that query without reading the cell

feedback.feedback: This is the clearest formulation of the lower-bound mechanism. It tells the reader why merely guessing or visiting cells still constitutes a simultaneous prediction of the address bits, without claiming that an algorithm must explicitly compute the address first.
feedback.why_it_matters: The position-versus-content distinction is what makes the direct-product theorem apply to arbitrary adaptive algorithms.
feedback.advice: Keep this sentence and the total-cap-to-separate-caps explanation. Do not shorten them back into a slogan that reaching a cell requires first learning its address.

locator.quote: $k=2$ gives exactly the cube.

feedback.feedback: The word exactly is too strong for the bounds being used. At k=2 the leading powers match a cubic comparison, but the lower-bound and upper-bound logarithms remain. The companion correctly says fixed k excludes exponents strictly below 4−2/k and does not provide an exact quartic separation.
feedback.why_it_matters: The phrase can undo the careful strict-exponent and logarithmic-loss discussion in the surrounding paragraph.
feedback.advice: Say that k=2 gives the cubic exponent at the level of the leading powers and does not refute the cubic bound. Keep k=3 as the concrete parameter that does refute it.

locator.quote: $k=4$ gives exactly $3.5$ and does not suffice

feedback.feedback: The answer conflates proving alpha_tot at least 3.5 with refuting a universal bound of exponent exactly 3.5. The question asks for the former. Fixed k=4 does suffice for that conclusion: for every alpha<3.5, d=2−1/4−alpha/2>0, so the displayed ratio diverges and no smaller exponent works. The same bounds do not establish divergence at alpha=3.5 itself; choosing k=5 does that stronger job.
feedback.why_it_matters: The exercise intended to teach strict inequalities instead teaches an incorrect implication about an infimum.
feedback.advice: Either change the question’s objective to ruling out R≤C(1+Q)^{3.5}, for which the given k=5 answer fits the argument, or say k=4 suffices for alpha_tot≥3.5 while k=5 excludes the endpoint bound. The main alpha_tot=4 proof is unaffected.

locator.section: §6: the fixed-parameter route and the companion
locator.quote: a $k$ that grows with $m$ cannot be substituted into these bounds

feedback.feedback: The qualification these bounds is correct, but a reader following the companion finds a later uniform-in-k estimate and a diagonal choice. The two documents can look contradictory unless the distinction between the fixed-k theorem used here and the stronger uniform input used there is made navigable.
feedback.why_it_matters: The funnel should make clear which extra estimate permits a different parameter choice, without making the exposition carry that proof.
feedback.advice: Add a short pointer saying that a growing-k construction requires additional uniform estimates, treated in the companion and record. Keep the present fixed-k proof as the exposition’s main route and keep the t≥2^k counterexample.

locator.quote: the record reconstructs it with the constant $35^4$

feedback.feedback: The constant 35^4 appears only in a final parenthesis and plays no role in why four is optimal. A newcomer has just completed the separation argument and is now asked to notice a numerical refinement of a theorem being imported.
feedback.why_it_matters: The ending shifts attention from the achieved conceptual payoff to an unused constant.
feedback.advice: Keep the citation and full-proof link for the universal quartic bound, but leave this constant to the record or companion unless a later use needs it.

locator.quote: There [$R$][def-R] is defined through [finite random mixtures][def-randomized] of [decision trees][def-tree]

feedback.feedback: The formal-verification section is much more appropriate after the last revision, but its first paragraph still contains a dense run of linked definitions and theorem variants. The genuinely useful novice entry, checking the winning condition on the changed board, comes only in the next paragraph.
feedback.why_it_matters: A reader looking for one meaningful formal check can mistake the link cluster for a required tour of the implementation vocabulary.
feedback.advice: Lead with the changed-board check and retain one link to the full statement file. Let the model-definition links be an optional second route. Preserve the plain statement of the one material difference, the unspecified logarithmic power, without adding receipt or review-status prose.

locator.section: Answers and exercises: what understanding is tested
locator.quote: What does one Grover iteration do here?

feedback.feedback: The four questions test local winning clauses, a deterministic next pivot, an independence calculation and a parameter inequality. None tests the new sampler’s unequal conditional distribution or asks the reader to distinguish a sampler failure from evidence that no winner exists. The current second question happens to end with a single surviving column and success after one Grover iteration.
feedback.why_it_matters: A student can answer all four questions while still treating the quantum algorithm as ordinary elimination with a magical speedup.
feedback.advice: Retarget or supplement Question 2 using the record’s abstract fractional example, with one loser pair set to probability 1/2 so that a genuinely fractional loser weight remains after the first pivot. Ask for the joint success masses and conditional pivot probabilities, or ask what a failure after listing the winner changes. State the abstract comparison-matrix scope explicitly.

locator.quote: A column that dominates the comparisons is therefore only a candidate

feedback.feedback: The changed pointer demonstrates a precise failure mode: comparison dominance alone does not certify a positive input. It motivates final verification using an actual malformed total-function input, rather than a warning detached from the construction.
feedback.why_it_matters: This is a robust teaching example that survives changes in the presentation of the sampler.
feedback.advice: Keep it before the algorithm’s correctness analysis, and return to its single failed pointer test when explaining verification. Its role differs from the domain-bit example and from the loser cycle.

locator.section: §4: the algorithm does not know its analytical weights
locator.quote: The weights are defined from the unknown probabilities $a_{ij}$; the algorithm never computes or estimates them.

feedback.feedback: This sentence prevents the most damaging operational misreading of the proof. The following sampler computes with coherent comparisons; the weights are quantities used to prove its distribution and progress.
feedback.why_it_matters: Without it, the claimed speedup can seem to assume free access to an m-by-m table of probabilities.
feedback.advice: Keep this sentence at the first introduction of weights and retain the exact success-and-column mass formula as its constructive explanation.

locator.quote: stopping cannot remove a listed column

feedback.feedback: This is the right explanation of the asymmetric failure analysis. The sampler can have tiny success mass after the winner is already listed; correctness depends on retaining the list, not on successfully completing every possible stage.
feedback.why_it_matters: It protects the all-input bounded-time algorithm from being confused with an unbounded search guaranteed to find another pivot.
feedback.advice: Keep the statement beside the stopping rule. If the coupling paragraph is shortened, preserve this temporal condition explicitly.

locator.quote: yet substituting $k=t$ asks for $t\ge2^t$, which never holds.

feedback.feedback: This elementary example makes a genuine quantifier-order error visible without importing more of the Forrelation proof. It is short, memorable and directly relevant to the temptation to set k as a function of m.
feedback.why_it_matters: An otherwise formal warning becomes an inference the intended reader can test independently.
feedback.advice: Keep it, while qualifying the neighboring statement to the fixed-k bounds actually used in this exposition. The companion’s uniform route can remain a linked extension.
